{{Short description|Equation to approximate pooled degrees of freedom}}
In [[statistics]] and [[propagation of uncertainty|uncertainty analysis]], the '''Welch–Satterthwaite equation''' is used to calculate an approximation to the effective [[degrees of freedom (statistics)|degrees of freedom]] of a [[linear combination]] of independent [[sample variance]]s, also known as the '''pooled degrees of freedom''',<ref>{{Cite book|last=Spellman, Frank R.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0W1mAQAAQBAJ&q=%22pooled+degrees+of+freedom%22&pg=PA174|title=Handbook of mathematics and statistics for the environment|others=Whiting, Nancy E.|date = 12 November 2013|isbn=978-1-4665-8638-3|location=Boca Raton|oclc=863225343}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Van Emden, H. F. (Helmut Fritz)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wOxoFIa7NeYC&q=%22pooled+degrees+of+freedom%22&pg=PA68|title=Statistics for terrified biologists|date=2008|publisher=Blackwell Pub|isbn=978-1-4443-0039-0|location=Malden, MA|oclc=317778677}}</ref> corresponding to the [[pooled variance]].

For {{math|''n''}} sample variances {{math|''s''<sub>''i''</sub><sup>2</sup> (''i'' {{=}} 1, ..., ''n'')}}, each respectively having {{math|''ν''<sub>''i''</sub>}} degrees of freedom, often one computes the linear combination.

:<math>
  \chi' = \sum_{i=1}^n k_i s_i^2.
</math>

where <math>k_i </math> are weights. These are real positive numbers, in some domains <math> k_i=\frac{1}{\nu_i+1}</math> may be used. In general, the [[probability distribution]] of {{math|''χ'''}} cannot be expressed analytically.  However, its distribution can be approximated by another [[chi-squared distribution]], whose effective degrees of freedom are given by the '''Welch–Satterthwaite equation'''

:<math>
 \nu_{\chi'} \approx \frac{\displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^n k_i s_i^2\right)^2}
                          {\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(k_i s_i^2)^2}
                                               {\nu_i}
                          }
</math>

There is ''no'' assumption that the underlying population variances {{math|''σ<sub>i</sub>''<sup>2</sup>}} are equal. This is known as the [[Behrens–Fisher problem]].

The result can be used to perform approximate [[statistical inference]] tests.  The simplest application of this equation is in performing [[Welch's t-test|Welch's ''t''-test]].

The original Welch–Satterthwaite equation is known to systematically underestimate the effective degrees of freedom when the component degrees of freedom {{math|''ν''<sub>''i''</sub>}} are not large. This bias arises because the derivation implicitly uses the large-sample approximation <math>\nu_i/(\nu_i+2) \approx 1</math> when representing the expected value of {{math|''s<sub>i</sub>''<sup>4</sup>}}. A bias-corrected estimator that accounts for the finite degrees of freedom of each component is given by<ref name="vonDavier2025">{{Cite journal |last=von Davier |first=M. |date=2025 |title=An Improved Satterthwaite (1941, 1946) Effective df Approximation |journal=Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics |volume=51 |issue=1 |doi=10.3102/10769986241309329}}</ref><ref name="vonDavier2026">{{Cite arXiv |last=von Davier |first=M. |date=2026 |title=A Corrected Welch Satterthwaite Equation. And: What You Always Wanted to Know About Kish's Effective Sample but Were Afraid to Ask |eprint=2602.20912 |class=stat.ME}}</ref>

:<math>
\nu_{\chi'}^{\text{(corr)}} \approx \frac{\displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^n k_i s_i^2\right)^2}
{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(k_i s_i^2)^2}
{\nu_i + 2}
} \;-\; 2.
</math>

As {{math|''ν''<sub>''i''</sub> → ∞}} for all components, the extra terms vanish and the corrected formula reduces to the original Welch–Satterthwaite equation. Simulation studies confirm that the corrected estimator closely matches the nominal degrees of freedom even for small component sizes, whereas the original equation exhibits severe downward bias.<ref name="vonDavier2026" />
